ledger.sentence: An X-ray uses a beam of electromagnetic radiation to make an image of the inside of the body.
According to the NHS, X-rays can produce images of many parts of the body, including bones, teeth, lungs and the digestive system.
They are used, for example, to check for broken bones after an accident.
A trust leaflet says that specially trained staff check each request first, to confirm the test is the right one for the person and their condition.
The health professional who takes X-rays in hospital is called a radiographer.
The radiographer positions the person sitting, lying or standing, depending on the part of the body.
ledger.note: Summary: positions you sitting, lying or standing.

ledger.sentence: The X-ray itself takes only a few minutes, according to the NHS.
The NHS says people are asked to remove metal items such as jewellery and zips.
Some types need fasting for several hours beforehand.
ledger.note: NHS X-ray page: not eat or drink for several hours before (for some types).

ledger.sentence: The NHS lists several related tests, including angiography, which checks blood vessels using a dye injected into the blood.
It also lists DEXA scans, which measure bone density, and CT scans, which give more detailed images.
Studies of the digestive system use a barium drink or enema, a liquid that shows up on X-ray.
After a dye or barium test, the NHS says people may be asked to wait for up to 30 minutes so staff can check for a reaction.
The NHS says X-rays are safe and serious complications are rare.
It adds that there is a very small risk of cancer linked to having lots of X-rays.
Trust leaflets say staff keep doses as low as possible and that a test goes ahead only when its benefit outweighs the small risk.
ledger.note: Summary: doses as low as possible; benefit outweighs small risk.

ledger.sentence: GOV.UK safety advice says that when imaging is properly justified and optimised, the risks from X-ray examinations are far smaller than the risks of the conditions being investigated.
It describes the added chance of cancer as very small, and says any effect would appear years or decades later.
The same advice says children have a higher lifetime risk from X-rays than adults, and that risk is lower for older patients because cancers take a long time to develop.
These leaflets give their own figures for the risk, and the figures differ between leaflets, so the radiographer or the doctor who requested the test is the person to ask.
ledger.note: Summary caveat: sources differ in numerical risk figures.

ledger.sentence: Trusts ask anyone who might be pregnant to tell the team before an X-ray.
A Leicester hospitals leaflet says X-rays during pregnancy do not increase the risk of miscarriage, birth defects or developmental problems.
The main concern it names is a very small increase in the chance that the baby develops cancer in childhood.
X-rays of the abdomen and pelvis are usually avoided in pregnancy.
X-rays of parts of the body well away from the abdomen, such as arms and legs, and dental X-rays, do not give any increased risk to an unborn baby, according to the same leaflet.
When an urgent test is needed, a radiologist and the doctor who asked for it decide together whether it should go ahead.
A reporting radiographer or a radiologist, a doctor who specialises in imaging, reviews the X-ray.
ledger.note: Summary: reviewed by reporting radiographer or radiologist.

ledger.sentence: The report goes to the team that requested the test.
The NHS says results may come on the same day or at an appointment a few weeks later, and that a clinician should explain them.
The wait varies with how urgent the X-ray is.
ledger.note: Summary: timeframe varies depending on urgency.

ledger.sentence: An X-ray can produce images of many parts of the body, and the NHS lists fractures, teeth, lungs and the digestive system among them.
The NHS describes X-rays as safe, with serious complications rare and a very small cancer risk linked to having lots of them.
Trust leaflets say X-rays in pregnancy do not raise the risk of miscarriage or birth defects, and that those of the abdomen and pelvis are usually avoided.
Results may be given on the same day or at an appointment some weeks later, depending on the type of X-ray.
An X-ray uses a small beam of radiation to picture bones, lungs and other parts. This guide covers the test, radiation risk, pregnancy and results.
ledger.note: Summary restates the supported sentences below.
